assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 500 req/s peak for an operator running ~500 lots. More than half the traffic is availability polling from display boards and the mobile app, not vehicles: actual gate events are ~140/s and only ~60/s of those are payments

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: Free-spot counts live in the cache and are the read path for every display board and app screen; the database is the system of record. The counter is decremented on entry and incremented on exit, so DRIFT between cache and database is a real failure mode - and it is not something this engine can model

assumptions.subject: pay
assumptions.statement: THE EXIT PAYMENT PATH IS THE BOTTLENECK AT 75%, not the app tier - which is the right answer for a parking system, because a queue at the exit barrier is a physical traffic jam. What is modelled is the payment service YOU run; the card acquirer is not a component, because a third-party API has no per-instance price (it is billed per transaction). Its 80 auth/s capacity is the contracted terminal/acquirer ceiling, each instance blocks on a ~120 ms round-trip, and queueing at 75% takes the pay_exit flow to ~530 ms mean and ~2.5 s at p99 against ~44 ms for an availability check

assumptions.subject: app
assumptions.statement: ~350 req/s per instance. Two instances is deliberately small: this is a genuinely small system and a reference design should not pretend otherwise

assumptions.subject: q
assumptions.statement: Gate and payment events fan out to display boards, billing and analytics through a 3-broker Kafka cluster. Three brokers is a QUORUM choice, not a capacity one (the cluster is ~1% busy). The consumers are not modelled - the v1 engine models request paths, not background workers

assumptions.subject: scope
assumptions.statement: ANPR cameras, barrier hardware, plate-image storage and the offline behaviour of a gate that loses its network are OUT OF SCOPE. Those are the hard parts of a real parking system and none of them is expressible in a request-path capacity model

assumptions.subject: cost
assumptions.statement: The load balancer is priced at 0: an ALB's hourly + LCU charge is per load balancer, not per instance, and the engine multiplies cost by instance count. Add ~$16/month plus LCU to any total you quote

_library.summary: Gate-scan ticketing with live spot counters, an event stream, and an exit-payment path that is the real constraint.
